manual.example-command.text: The same tunnel, opened by hand from this machine with the ssh command, would be:
manual.example-intro.text: Take a Host at {host}, registered with the user {user}, and a service port whose Service IP and Service port are {service}, an address tunnel-manager can reach, and whose Local port is {local_port}. The numbers on the drawing are these four steps:
manual.example-step-1.text: tunnel-manager opens an SSH connection to {host} port 22 and signs in as {user}. This is the only connection that is opened between the two machines, and it is opened from here: the Host opens nothing back, so nothing has to be reachable on this machine.
manual.example-step-2.text: Over that connection the SSH server on the Host opens port {local_port} on the Host. A client anywhere that can reach the Host connects to {host}:{local_port}.
manual.example-step-3.text: That connection is carried back down the same SSH connection to tunnel-manager.
manual.example-step-4.text: tunnel-manager connects to {service} and passes the traffic through. The client is talking to the service, and neither of them has the address of the other.
manual.forward-diagram-port.label: Local port
manual.forward-diagram-target.label: The target
manual.forward-diagram.aria: Drawing of one local forward: tunnel-manager opens an SSH connection to the Host and a local port on this machine, a client connects to that port, the connection runs over the SSH connection to the Host, and the Host connects to the target
manual.forward-direction.text: A local forward is what ssh -L does, kept up the way a tunnel is. tunnel-manager opens the local port on this machine, and every connection made to it is carried over the SSH connection of the Host and made again from the Host to the target IP and target port. The target is reached from the Host, so it can be an address only the Host sees, and 127.0.0.1 there is the Host itself.
manual.forward-example.text: Take a Host at {host} carrying a local forward whose local port is {port} and whose target is {target}, an address the Host reaches. The numbers on the drawing are these four steps:
manual.forward-port.text: A local port is unique on this machine, whichever Host carries it. A port that another local forward or the SOCKS5 proxy of any Host opens, or the port this server listens on, is refused and nothing is stored.
manual.forward-scope.text: Where the port is opened is about this machine, not the Host. Every interface, the default, opens it on 0.0.0.0 and ::, and makes this machine a door into the network of the Host: anybody who reaches this machine on that port reaches the target without signing in to the Host, because the SSH login is the one tunnel-manager made. Choose This machine alone unless another machine is meant to use the forward, and put a firewall in front of the port when one is.
manual.forward-sshd.text: The SSH server of the Host has to allow forwarding in this direction. OpenSSH refuses it where AllowTcpForwarding is no or remote.
manual.forward-status-connected.text: connected: the SSH connection stands and the local port is open. It does not say the target answers: each connection is made from the Host on its own, and one that cannot reach the target is closed with the reason in the log.
manual.forward-status-disabled.text: disabled: the Host is disabled, and nothing is opened.
manual.forward-status-error.text: error: the last attempt failed, and the reason is shown under the row. After a refused login or a refused host key it waits until the Host is changed or the key is approved, and otherwise it is tried again after the monitoring interval.
manual.forward-status-reconnecting.text: reconnecting: the connection dropped or an attempt failed, and it is being made again.
manual.forward-status.text: The Status column of the list says how each forward stands. Local forwards are not counted on the Status screen.
manual.forward-step-1.text: tunnel-manager opens an SSH connection to {host}, and once it stands opens port {port} on this machine. The port is open only while that connection stands.
manual.forward-step-2.text: A client that can reach this machine connects to port {port} on it.
manual.forward-step-3.text: That connection is carried over the same SSH connection to the Host.
manual.forward-step-4.text: The SSH server of the Host connects to {target} and passes the traffic through. The target sees the connection come from the Host.
manual.forward-where.text: Local forwards are added, changed and deleted from the Local forwards button in the row of a Host on the Hosts screen. A forward runs while its Host is enabled, and deleting the Host deletes its forwards with it.
manual.forward.title: Local forwards
manual.one-tunnel-columns.text: The Status screen shows the three addresses of a tunnel in three columns: Server is the Host that was connected to, Local is the port opened on that Host, and Remote is the service the traffic is passed to.
manual.one-tunnel-dials.text: tunnel-manager is the end that dials. It opens the SSH connection to the Host and the Host never opens one to it, so nothing has to be opened towards this machine for a tunnel to stand. The traffic then runs the other way down that connection, from the Host to the service.
manual.one-tunnel.title: How one tunnel is built
manual.parts-assignment.text: An assignment is one Host paired with one service port. It says that this Host is to carry this service port.
manual.parts-built-from.text: The assignment is what a tunnel is built from. One stands for every assignment whose Host is enabled and for no other pair, so a Host with no assignment runs nothing however many service ports are registered, and a service port assigned to no Host is carried nowhere.
manual.parts-disabling.text: Disabling a Host keeps its assignments. Its tunnels are stopped, and enabling it again brings the same set of them back.
manual.parts-host.text: A Host is an SSH endpoint: its address, its SSH port, the user to sign in as, and the private key or the password to sign in with. It carries a switch of its own, and a Host that is not enabled runs no tunnels.
manual.parts-local-forward.text: A local forward belongs to one Host and runs the other way from a tunnel: this machine opens the port, and each connection to it goes on from the Host to an address the Host reaches. It needs no assignment, and is added from the Local forwards button in the row of its Host.
manual.parts-service-port.text: A service port is both ends of one forward: the Service IP and the Service port are the address tunnel-manager connects to, which is any address it can reach and not only one on its own machine, and the Local port is the port the listener is opened on, on the Host.
manual.parts-socks.text: A SOCKS5 proxy also belongs to one Host and runs the same way as a local forward, except that the browser names where each connection goes, so one port reaches whatever the Host reaches. It is switched on with a tick in the add and edit forms of the Host.
manual.parts-three.text: Three things are stored, and a tunnel needs all three.
manual.parts-where.text: Assignments are made on the Hosts screen: the Service ports button in a row opens the list of every service port with the ones that Host carries checked, and a box checked or cleared there is what is saved. A Host and a service port are both registered carrying everything unless the box on the add form is cleared.
manual.parts.title: Hosts, service ports and assignments
manual.paths-absolute.text: A path that begins with / is used as it stands.
manual.paths-relative.text: Anything else is read against the directory the database file is in, which is the directory this whole installation lives in. It is never read against the directory the process was started from: that is not the same twice, so a relative path read against it would put the key or the log somewhere different on every start.
manual.paths-startup.text: The startup writes the absolute path of the database file, of the key file and of the log file it opened into the log, so the log always says which files are in use. The Settings screen names that directory under each of the two boxes.
manual.paths-two.text: Two settings hold a path, the encryption key file and the log file, and both are read the same way.
manual.paths-windows.text: On Windows a path counts as absolute only when it names a drive or a share, as in C:\tunnel-manager\logs\tunnel-manager.log. One that begins with a single backslash does not count, and is read against the installation directory like any other relative path.
manual.paths.title: Where a path in a setting points
manual.periods-answer.text: Because the answer to a change is sent before the tunnel exists, a change that was stored does not mean the tunnel came up. The Status screen is what answers that.
manual.periods-monitoring.text: The monitoring interval is how often a tunnel that is already up is checked. tunnel-manager reaches the SSH server of the Host and asks whether the connection is still answering, and builds it again when it is not. Shorter notices a connection that died sooner and reaches the Host more often.
manual.periods-next-start.text: Both are taken up at the next start, the way nearly every setting is. The log level is the one that takes hold the moment it is saved.
manual.periods-reconcile.text: The reconcile interval is how often the tunnels that are running are compared with what is stored. One that should be running and is not is started, one that should not be is stopped, and one whose settings changed is stopped and started again with the new ones.
manual.periods-startup.text: A reconcile pass also runs at the startup, before the API answers anything, and again right after a change is stored, so adding a Host or an assignment takes effect at once rather than at the next tick. The period is what tries again whatever a failed pass left undone.
manual.periods-two.text: Two periods are on the Settings screen, five seconds each to begin with, and they do different jobs.
manual.periods.title: The monitoring period and the reconcile period
manual.reach-column.text: The Port reached column of the Status screen is what came of trying it. Once a tunnel is up, tunnel-manager opens a TCP connection to the Host at that port and reports whether it answered: reachable, unreachable, or unknown while nothing has been measured. It is measured when the tunnel comes up and again on every reconnect, rather than on every reading of the screen, because what decides it is the configuration of the SSH server and that does not change under a connection that stands.
manual.reach-listener.text: The listener on the Host is opened by the SSH server of the Host and not by tunnel-manager. tunnel-manager asks for 0.0.0.0, which is every address of that machine, and which address is really bound is that server's decision: OpenSSH left at its default of GatewayPorts no, and Dropbear started without -a, bind loopback alone, and the port then answers on the Host itself and nowhere else.
manual.reach-unreachable.text: unreachable says where the port was not reached from, not why it was not. A server that bound the port to loopback alone and a firewall dropping the connection on the way look exactly the same from here, and a connection that never arrives cannot tell them apart. Check both before changing either. The Status screen writes what to look at under the row, and names the SSH server out of the banner it sent on the handshake.
manual.reach.title: How far the forwarded port is open
manual.screen.title: Manual
manual.socks-browser.text: To use it, point the browser at this machine. With the proxy on {address}:
manual.socks-chrome-loopback.text: Chrome does not send a loopback address such as 127.0.0.1 to a proxy. To reach a page the Host serves on its own loopback address, start it with this as well:
manual.socks-chrome.text: Chrome: start it with the proxy on its command line.
manual.socks-connect.text: The proxy speaks the CONNECT of SOCKS5 alone, to an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a name. BIND and UDP ASSOCIATE are answered as not supported, a client that offers only a username and a password is refused, and SOCKS4 is closed without an answer.
manual.socks-firefox.text: Firefox: Settings, Network Settings, Manual proxy configuration. Put the address and the port in SOCKS Host and Port, pick SOCKS v5, and tick Proxy DNS when using SOCKS v5, so that names are resolved by the Host and not by the machine the browser runs on.
manual.socks-open.text: The proxy asks for no password, and it is opened on every interface unless you choose otherwise, so anybody who reaches this machine on its port reaches the network of the Host. Chrome and Firefox have no place to give a SOCKS5 proxy a password, so fill in Allowed client addresses, as in 203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.7, and put a firewall in front of the port. A client from an address that is not on the list is closed at once.
manual.socks-switch.text: It is switched on with the Turn on a SOCKS5 proxy tick in the add and edit forms of a Host on the Hosts screen. The port, where it is opened and the Allowed client addresses box appear once the tick is on, and the port starts at 1080. The SOCKS5 proxy column of the list shows the port and how it stands, in the same words as a local forward. The port is held to the same rule as a local port: one that a local forward, another proxy or this server holds is refused.
manual.socks-what.text: A SOCKS5 proxy is what ssh -D does, kept up the way a local forward is. This machine opens the SOCKS5 port, a browser set to use it asks for a site, and the connection to that site is made from the Host over its SSH connection. A name is passed to the Host and resolved there, so a name only the network of the Host knows works as well.
manual.socks.title: SOCKS5 proxy
manual.step-host.text: Over that connection the SSH server of the Host is asked to open a listener on the Host itself, at the local port of the service port. It stands for as long as the connection does.
manual.step-host.title: The Host
manual.step-manager.text: Opens an SSH connection out to the Host and signs in as the user registered for it, with the key or the password stored beside it.
manual.step-manager.title: tunnel-manager
manual.step-service.text: Whatever connects to that port on the Host is carried back down the same SSH connection, and tunnel-manager dials the service and passes it on.
manual.step-service.title: The service
manual.what-it-does-keeps.text: tunnel-manager keeps a set of SSH tunnels standing. Each one opens a port on a Host you registered here, and whatever connects to that port is carried to a service that tunnel-manager dials on its behalf.
manual.what-it-does-nothing.text: Nothing is installed on the Host. tunnel-manager uses the SSH server the Host already runs, connecting to it the way a person at a terminal would.

restart.ask-moved.confirm: Restart tunnel-manager? Every tunnel is cut and the API stops answering while the service goes down and comes up again. It comes back on its own within seconds. It comes back at {address}, which is what the settings waiting for this restart say, so this page goes there once it has had time to come up.
restart.ask-same.confirm: Restart tunnel-manager? Every tunnel is cut and the API stops answering while the service goes down and comes up again. It comes back on its own within seconds, at the same address.
restart.ask-stops.confirm: Restart tunnel-manager? Every tunnel is cut and the API stops answering while the service goes down and comes up again. This platform cannot start the program again by itself: bringing it back is left to whatever supervises this service, and if it was started by hand it does not come back.
restart.asked-many.text: The restart was asked for. The service stops answering about {seconds} seconds after this screen appeared, every tunnel comes down with it and is built again on the way back.
restart.asked-one.text: The restart was asked for. The service stops answering about {seconds} second after this screen appeared, every tunnel comes down with it and is built again on the way back.
restart.card.text: A restart is what puts a stored setting that waits for one into place. The API stops answering, every tunnel comes down and is built again afterwards, so everything going through a tunnel is cut for as long as the restart takes.
restart.card.title: Restart the service
restart.gave-up.notice: The service did not answer again within {seconds} seconds. Check the server.
restart.in-place-moved.text: This process runs the program again in place of itself. It keeps the process it already is, so the service is back within seconds and nothing has to start it. It comes back at {address}, which is not where this page is, so this page goes there rather than waiting here for something that is not coming.
restart.in-place-same.text: This process runs the program again in place of itself. It keeps the process it already is, so the service is back within seconds and nothing has to start it. It answers at the same address it does now.
restart.moving-many.empty: If the service does not come back at this address, this page opens {address} in {seconds} seconds.
restart.moving-one.empty: If the service does not come back at this address, this page opens {address} in {seconds} second.
restart.screen.title: Restarting
restart.stops.text: This platform cannot replace the image of a running process, so the restart ends with the process stopped. Whatever supervises the service is what starts it again, and a service that was started by hand does not come back at all.
restart.stuck.text: Nothing further happens on this page. Reload it once the service is running again.
restart.unknown.notice: What a restart would do could not be read, so it is not offered here: {reason}
restart.waiting-many.empty: Waiting for the service to answer again. This page asks every {every} seconds and gives up after {limit} seconds.
restart.waiting-one.empty: Waiting for the service to answer again. This page asks every {every} second and gives up after {limit} seconds.

settings.pending-restart.notice: A restart is what puts them into place. What it does on this machine, and what is cut while it runs, is on the Restart the service card further down this screen.
settings.pending-where.notice: Restart the service, further down this screen, is what puts them into place.
settings.pending.text: These settings are stored with a value this service is not running on. It goes on running on what it read when it started until it is started again.

settings.reconcile.hint: How often the tunnels that are running are compared with the Hosts and service ports that are registered. A tunnel that should exist is started, one that should not is stopped, and one whose settings changed is built again. Taken up at the next start.
settings.reconcile.label: Reconcile interval (seconds)
settings.rescue-kept.text: Only the settings go back. The registered Hosts, the service ports, the account and the certificate are left as they are, so nothing has to be registered again and you log in with the password you already have.
settings.rescue.text: Start it once with -reset-settings. Every setting goes back to its default, what it changed is printed, and the process exits. The next start runs on the defaults, and this screen is reachable again.

status.addresses-answer-no-proof.text: What a server answers to a request is not a measurement of what it bound. A server set to bind every interface takes both families on the first request and says no to the second, so a request it said no to can still be a port that is up.
status.addresses-answered-both.text: The SSH server said yes to both requests.
status.addresses-answered-ipv4.text: The SSH server said yes to the IPv4 request and no to the IPv6 one.
status.addresses-answered-ipv6.text: The SSH server said yes to the IPv6 request and no to the IPv4 one.
status.addresses-asked-one.text: Asked for at {address} on the Host.
status.addresses-asked-pair.text: Asked for at {first} and {second} on the Host.
status.addresses-confirmed-none.text: Nothing is confirmed from here: no address of this forward has answered a connection opened by tunnel-manager.
status.addresses-confirmed-plain.text: Confirmed from here: the forwarded port answered a connection opened by tunnel-manager.
status.addresses-confirmed.text: Confirmed from here: {address} answered a connection opened by tunnel-manager.
status.addresses-host-only.text: Nothing here can confirm it. These addresses are on the Host itself, which nothing outside that system reaches, so whether the ports are up there is not something this program can measure.
status.addresses-known.text: What is known about the addresses of this forward
status.addresses-listening.text: Answered by the Host: this port is listening at {addresses}.
status.all-connected.notice: Every tunnel that should be running is connected.
status.connected.label: Connected
status.denied-authorized-keys.text: The key this Host is logged in with may carry a restriction of its own. A line in authorized_keys that starts with no-port-forwarding or restrict refuses this whatever the server settings say.
status.denied-cause.text: The refusal came from the Host and carries no reason with it, so what follows is what makes a server refuse, likeliest first. None of it can be read as the cause from here.
status.denied-forwarding.text: The Host may have remote forwarding turned off. On OpenSSH that is AllowTcpForwarding, which has to be yes or remote, and DisableForwarding, which has to be off.
status.denied-in-use.text: Something on the Host may already hold the port, an earlier connection of this program that has not been let go among it.
status.denied-permitlisten.text: The Host may allow only certain ports to be opened. On OpenSSH that is PermitListen, and a port outside its list is refused the same way.
status.denied-privileged.text: Port {port} is below 1024, which on Linux and macOS is opened only by root. The account this Host is registered with may not be one.
status.denied.text: The SSH server refused to open this port.
status.desired.label: Desired
status.down-many.notice: {count} tunnels have rows but are not connected.
status.down-one.notice: {count} tunnel has a row but is not connected.
status.host-key-approved.notice: Host {id} is trusted on {fingerprint} from now on. Its tunnels are built again.
status.host-key-changed.text: The SSH server presented a host key other than the one this Host is trusted on. Either the server was rebuilt and given a new key, or this connection is not reaching the server it is meant for. Find out which before approving the key that was presented: the key approved here is what every connection to this Host is checked against, and the password of the Host is offered to whatever answers on it.
status.host-key-first.text: No host key has been approved for this Host yet, so every connection to it is refused. Compare the fingerprint below with the one the server itself reports, which is what ssh-keygen -lf prints for its host key file, and approve it to let the tunnels connect.
status.host-key-gone.text: There is no host key waiting to be approved for this Host. Either it has been approved already, or nothing has connected to this Host since the last one was.
status.host-key-mismatch.notice: The SSH server presented a host key other than the one this Host is trusted on, so the connection was refused before any password or key was offered.
status.host-key-password.error: Enter the password this account is signed in with.
status.host-key-password.hint: The password this account is signed in with. Replacing a key that is trusted asks for it, so that a screen left open cannot trust another key by itself.
status.host-key-password.label: Account password
status.host-key-presented.label: Presented now
status.host-key-trusted.label: Trusted now
status.host-key-unapproved.notice: No host key has been approved for this Host, so the connection was refused before any password or key was offered.
status.host-key.title: Host key of Host {id} ({ip})
status.host-keys-all.hint: A Host that presented a key other than the one it is trusted on is left out of this. Approving a first key is a step of registering a Host, and there are as many of them as there are Hosts; replacing a trusted one says that the server itself changed, which is worth a row of its own.
status.host-keys-all.label: Check every Host on this page that has never been approved
status.host-keys-approved-many.notice: {count} host keys were approved. The tunnels of those Hosts are built again.
status.host-keys-approved-one.notice: {count} host key was approved. The tunnels of that Host are built again.
status.host-keys-changed-many.notice: {count} of them presented a key other than the one they are trusted on.
status.host-keys-changed-one.notice: {count} of them presented a key other than the one it is trusted on.
status.host-keys-chosen-many.text: {count} Hosts are checked, on this page and on the ones before it.
status.host-keys-chosen-one.text: {count} Host is checked, on this page and on the ones before it.
status.host-keys-confirm-changed.text: Some of these Hosts are trusted on another key already, and approving them drops the key that would have caught a server answering in their place. Each of those rows carries both fingerprints. The password of this account is asked for below because of them.
status.host-keys-confirm.text: These are the Hosts that are about to be approved and the key each of them will be trusted on from then on. Some of them were checked on pages you have turned away from, so read the list through before approving it.
status.host-keys-confirm.title: Approve these host keys
status.host-keys-none.error: Check the Hosts whose fingerprints you have compared with their servers.
status.host-keys-refused.notice: {approved} approved, {refused} refused. The rows that were refused are below, each with what it met.
status.host-keys-waiting-many.notice: {count} Hosts are waiting for their host keys to be approved, so their tunnels are not connecting.
status.host-keys-waiting-one.notice: {count} Host is waiting for its host key to be approved, so its tunnels are not connecting.
status.host-keys.text: Each Host below refused every connection because the key its SSH server presented has not been approved. Compare the fingerprint in a row with the one the server itself reports, which is what ssh-keygen -lf prints for its host key file, and check the row. What is checked stays checked as you turn the pages, and the button at the bottom lists all of it once more before anything is approved.
status.host-keys.title: Host keys waiting to be approved
status.missing-many.notice: {count} tunnels that should be running have no row yet.
status.missing-one.notice: {count} tunnel that should be running has no row yet.
status.reach-address.text: Connected, but {address} did not answer a connection from tunnel-manager.
status.reach-anywhere.text: Connected, but the forwarded port did not answer a connection from tunnel-manager.
status.reach-cause.text: This says where the port was not reached from, not why it was not. Two things look the same from here and neither is ruled out: the SSH server may have bound the forwarded port to loopback only, or a firewall between this machine and the Host may be dropping the connection. Check both.
status.reach-dropbear-all.text: Dropbear has no middle value. -a opens every forwarded port to all addresses and leaving it out keeps them on loopback; there is nothing that lets the client choose the address, the way GatewayPorts clientspecified does on OpenSSH.
status.reach-dropbear-flag.text: The flag goes where the arguments of the service are, the init script or the unit file that starts Dropbear, and Dropbear is restarted for it.
status.reach-dropbear.text: If it is the SSH server: Dropbear is told this with the -a flag on its command line, not by a setting in a configuration file.
status.reach-firewall.text: If it is the firewall: the port has to be open through whatever sits between this machine and the Host, which may be a firewall on the Host itself, a security group, or something on the way. A port the SSH server did open is still not reached while that is closed, so this is worth checking even after the server has been changed.
status.reach-no-banner.text: The SSH server sent no version banner, so there is nothing here that says what it is.
status.reach-openssh-order.text: Where the line goes decides whether it counts. sshd_config usually carries an Include of sshd_config.d/*.conf, and OpenSSH keeps the first value it reads for a setting, so a GatewayPorts added at the bottom is ignored when an included file already set one above it. Change the first GatewayPorts on that path, not the last.
status.reach-openssh-restart.text: Check the configuration with sshd -t before restarting, then restart the server: sshd reads its configuration when it starts.
status.reach-openssh.text: If it is the SSH server: OpenSSH keeps a forwarded port on loopback unless GatewayPorts says otherwise. This tunnel asks for 0.0.0.0, and GatewayPorts clientspecified in sshd_config is what allows that.
status.reach-other.text: The banner names neither OpenSSH nor Dropbear, so what opens a forwarded port on this server is not known from here. Its own documentation is what says whether it has such a setting and what it is called.

transfer.card.text: An export hands out a file and an import takes one back, so neither installation has to reach the other and you decide where the file is kept and for how long. The file is encrypted with a password you type here; it is stored nowhere, so a file whose password is forgotten cannot be opened by anyone, this program included.
transfer.card.title: Carry this configuration to another installation
transfer.drop.label: Drop the exported file here, or paste it into the box above.
transfer.export-settings-sealed.text: The settings hold no password of their own, and the file is encrypted all the same: it is one format and one thing to explain, and a second format that happens not to need a password today is the one somebody puts a secret into tomorrow.
transfer.export-settings.text: The stored settings go into one file: the API port and whether HTTPS is served, the two intervals, where the encryption key is kept, and everything about the log. The account, the certificate and the Hosts are not in it.
transfer.export-settings.title: Export the settings of the manager
transfer.export-tunnels.notice: The file is encrypted with the password typed here, and that password is the only thing protecting it. Inside the file, the SSH password, the private key and the key passphrase of every Host are written as plain text, because the database keeps them encrypted with the key of this machine and that key never leaves it: a file that carried them in that form could not be read on any other installation. Whoever has both the file and its password has the SSH credentials of every Host named in it. Keep it where you keep secrets.
transfer.export-tunnels.text: Every Host and every service port registered here goes into one file, which this browser saves. Nothing is left on the server.
transfer.export-tunnels.title: Export the tunnel configuration
transfer.exported-host-many-port-many.no: The browser is saving {name}. It holds {hosts} Hosts and {ports} service ports, with the SSH credentials of every one of those Hosts inside it. Keep it where you keep secrets.
transfer.exported-host-many-port-one.not: The browser is saving {name}. It holds {hosts} Hosts and {ports} service port, with the SSH credentials of every one of those Hosts inside it. Keep it where you keep secrets.
transfer.exported-host-one-port-many.not: The browser is saving {name}. It holds {hosts} Host and {ports} service ports, with the SSH credentials of every one of those Hosts inside it. Keep it where you keep secrets.
transfer.exported-host-one-port-one.noti: The browser is saving {name}. It holds {hosts} Host and {ports} service port, with the SSH credentials of every one of those Hosts inside it. Keep it where you keep secrets.
transfer.exported-settings.notice: The browser is saving {name}. It holds the settings that are stored here.
transfer.file-example.hint: One long line of text, which an export handed out
transfer.file-password.error: Enter the password the file was encrypted with at the export.
transfer.file-password.hint: The password that was typed at the export, not the password of this account.
transfer.file-password.label: Password of the file
transfer.file.error: Paste the file an export handed out, or drop it onto the area below.
transfer.file.hint: A dropped file is read in this browser and sent as text, exactly as a paste would be. The file itself is not uploaded.
transfer.file.label: The exported file
transfer.import-atomic.text: The whole import is one write. If any row of the file is refused, none of it is stored and this installation is left exactly as it was, so there is nothing to undo before correcting the file and importing it again.
transfer.import-empty.notice: The file was read. It holds no Host and no service port.
transfer.import-settings-one-row.text: A setting the file does not name is left as it is here. There is no box to check: the settings are one row, so an import of them is a replacement either way.
transfer.import-settings.text: The settings the file holds are stored, and none of them is put onto the running service, the API port and HTTPS included. What is stored is what the next start runs on, and until then it is listed at the top of this screen as waiting for a restart. That is what keeps a file from another machine moving the port out from under the screen you are reading.
transfer.import-settings.title: Import settings of a manager
transfer.import-tunnels.text: A Host or a service port the file holds and this installation does not is added. One that is registered here already is skipped and named below, unless the box at the bottom of this card is checked.
transfer.import-tunnels.title: Import a tunnel configuration
transfer.imported-skipped.notice: The file was imported: {added} added, {replaced} replaced, {skipped} skipped. What was skipped is registered here already, with the reason against each row in the table on the card. Check the box and import the same file again to store the file's version of those rows instead.
transfer.imported.notice: The file was imported: {added} added, {replaced} replaced, {skipped} skipped. The table on the card says what became of every row of it.
transfer.items-none.empty: That file held no Host and no service port.
transfer.items.title: What the last import did
transfer.kinds.text: There are two kinds of file: one holds the Hosts with their service ports, the other holds the settings of this manager. Each import reads only its own kind, and a file of the other kind is refused with a message naming which kind it turned out to hold.
transfer.overwrite.hint: Cleared, an import only adds: a Host or a service port that is registered here already is skipped, so nothing is overwritten by accident. Checked, such a row is updated from the file instead. The row that is here is updated in place rather than replaced, so the tunnels of that Host reconnect instead of being created again from the start.
transfer.overwrite.label: Replace what is registered here
transfer.password-again.hint: Type it a second time. A slip at the keyboard is caught here rather than at the import, where the file would not open and nothing would say why.
transfer.password-again.label: Password again
transfer.password.hint: It encrypts the file and is the only thing that opens it again. It is typed again at the import, and it is stored nowhere.
transfer.password.label: Password for the file
transfer.settings-stored-many.notice: The settings are stored. {count} of them are waiting for a restart and are listed at the top of this screen, where the restart that puts them into place is. Nothing was put onto the running service.
transfer.settings-stored-one.notice: The settings are stored. {count} of them is waiting for a restart and is listed at the top of this screen, where the restart that puts them into place is. Nothing was put onto the running service.
transfer.settings-unchanged.notice: The settings in that file are the ones stored here already. Nothing changed.
uninstall.ask.confirm: Uninstall tunnel-manager? The database, the encryption key and the logs are removed and the process stops.
uninstall.file-database.text: The database file, along with the -wal and -shm files SQLite keeps beside it
uninstall.file-initial-password.text: The initial password file, if it is still there
uninstall.file-logs.text: The log file and the rotated log files beside it
uninstall.form.title: Dangerous actions
uninstall.intro.text: Uninstall stops every tunnel, removes the files this installation is made of and ends the process. Nothing here can be taken back.
uninstall.key.text: Removing the encryption key is the part nothing undoes. The SSH password of every Host is encrypted with that key, so a backup of the database taken beforehand cannot be read once the key is gone: the passwords in it stay unreadable and have to be typed in again on a fresh installation.
uninstall.password.error: Enter the password of this account.
uninstall.password.hint: The password this account is signed in with. It is asked for again so that a screen left open cannot be uninstalled with one press.
uninstall.password.label: Password
uninstall.program.text: The program file is left where it is. A running process cannot remove its own image on every system this runs on, so removing it is left to you once the process has stopped.
uninstalled.left.notice: These could not be removed and are still on disk. Remove them by hand.
uninstalled.left.title: Left behind
uninstalled.no-answer.text: This screen is drawn from what the uninstall answered, and this page holds no answer. If the uninstall ran, the server is gone and there is nothing left to ask.
uninstalled.none.empty: No file was there to remove.
uninstalled.program.text: The program file is still where it was. Remove it by hand, along with the service entry that starts it, if this installation was set up as a service.
uninstalled.removed.title: Removed
uninstalled.screen.title: Uninstalled
uninstalled.stopped-many.text: Every tunnel was stopped, the database was closed and the files below were removed. The process stops about {seconds} seconds after this screen appeared. Reloading this page will not bring it back.
uninstalled.stopped-one.text: Every tunnel was stopped, the database was closed and the files below were removed. The process stops about {seconds} second after this screen appeared. Reloading this page will not bring it back.
uninstalled.stopped-soon.text: Every tunnel was stopped, the database was closed and the files below were removed. The process stops a few seconds after this screen appeared. Reloading this page will not bring it back.

update.auto-install.label: Install a newer release without asking
update.auto-install.notice: A newer release is installed as soon as it is found, and nobody is asked first. Leave this off unless a service that goes down at a time nobody picked is all right here.
update.check-enabled.hint: One request to the public release API, on the timer below. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is stored.

update.check-failed.notice: The newest release could not be read: {reason}. This is not the same as being up to date.
update.confirm-restart.text: The service is restarted at the end of it, which takes every tunnel down until it is up again. It cannot be stopped from here once it starts.
update.confirm.text: {tag} is downloaded, checked against the checksums the release publishes, and put in place of the executable this service runs.

update.install-failed.notice: The install did not go through: {version} is still running.
update.installed-other.notice: The install was started for {wanted}, and what is running now is {version}.
update.installed.notice: The install went through: {version} is running.

update.interval.hint: From 1 to 8760. Releases are not a thing that happens by the minute.

update.latest.label: Newest release
update.never-checked.empty: No check has been made yet. The timer checks on its own, and the button below checks now.
update.newer.notice: {tag} has been released, which is newer than what is running here.
update.not-comparable.notice: The newest release is {tag}, which is not a version this can compare with the one running. Nothing is installed on its own while that is so: what starts an install is a version read as newer, and one that cannot be read is not that.
update.not-installable.notice: An update cannot be installed from this screen. This program is running as something somebody started rather than as a registered service, so nothing would bring it back after the executable was replaced. The newest release is still shown above.
update.password.error: Enter the password of your account.
update.password.hint: It is asked for because the executable is replaced and every tunnel comes down with the restart.
update.password.label: Password of your account
update.running.label: Running
update.screen.text: What this installation is running, and what the newest release is. The version below is read on a timer rather than as this screen is drawn, so opening it costs nothing on the other side. The button asks now.
update.screen.title: Update
update.settings.title: When to check, and what to do about it
update.started-progress.aria: How much of the wait has gone by
update.started-reload.text: The version at the foot of the screen is what says the install went through.
update.started-waiting.text: This page waits here and loads itself again as soon as a different version answers. It stops waiting after {seconds} seconds and loads itself anyway, which puts the version that is running back on the screen.
update.started.text: The release is being downloaded and checked, and the service is restarted once it is in place. This screen is not told when that finishes: the process that would tell it is the one being restarted.
update.started.title: Installing
